did_you_know.text: The opening verse is the psalm’s title: it states that the psalm is intended for the chief musician and attributed to David.
The heavens and the sky are described as telling and proclaiming the glory of the Lord, even though this is not human speech.
The verse presents a continuous cycle of testimony: day speaks forth a message, and night conveys knowledge.
The message of the heavens is described as universal: it goes out through all the earth and reaches the ends of the world, without relying on an audible voice.
The sun is compared to a bridegroom coming out of his chamber and to a strong man rejoicing to run his course—images that emphasize joy, strength, and movement.
The sun’s path is described as extending from one end of the heavens to the other, and the verse emphasizes that nothing is hidden from its heat.
In the second part of the psalm, several terms are used for the word of the Lord: law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear of the Lord, and judgments.

The word of the Lord is credited with various effects on people: the law restores the soul, the testimony makes the simple wise, the precepts bring joy to the heart, and the commandment enlightens the eyes.
The word of the Lord is described as extremely valuable and especially sweet: more desirable than gold, even much fine gold, and sweeter than honey, even honey from the honeycomb.
The psalmist recognizes that people do not always understand their own errors, and therefore asks to be cleansed from hidden faults.
